Summarise each group down to one row

Source: R/summarise.R
summarise.tbl_gpu.Rd

summarise() computes one row per group of a GPU table (or one row in all, when it is ungrouped), as dplyr::summarise() does. The aggregations listed below run on the GPU; any other expression is evaluated by dplyr on the CPU (set options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn") to be told when and why; see cuplyr-fallback).

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
summarise(.data, ..., .groups = NULL, .by = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
summarize(.data, ..., .groups = NULL, .by = NULL)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu, usually grouped with group_by().

...

Name-value pairs of summary functions. The name will be the name of the variable in the result. The value is an aggregation expression in the form fun(column), where column can also be an expression of columns (see "Aggregation sub-expressions" below), or arithmetic around such calls and the results of earlier expressions (see "Arithmetic around reducers" below).

.groups

Grouping structure of the result, as in dplyr::summarise(). One of:

  • NULL (default): "drop_last", with a message when the result is still grouped (see "The regroup message" below).

  • "drop_last": drop the last grouping variable and keep the rest (group_by(a, b, c) gives a result grouped by a, b); with only one grouping variable, the result is ungrouped.

  • "drop": the result is ungrouped.

  • "keep": every grouping variable is kept.

  • "rowwise": the summary runs on the GPU keeping every grouping variable, and the result is a rowwise tbl_gpu by those variables (dplyr::rowwise()); collect() returns dplyr's own rowwise_df.

On a rowwise tbl_gpu (see rowwise.tbl_gpu()) summarise() computes one row per input row, the rowwise variables first. .groups = NULL (and "keep") groups the result by those variables (with dplyr's message when .groups is not given), "drop" ungroups it, "rowwise" keeps it rowwise; "drop_last" is an error, as in dplyr. On an ungrouped .data, as in dplyr, .groups is not checked: any value other than "rowwise" (a typo included) is ignored.

The regroup message

When .groups is NULL and .data has more than one grouping variable, summarise() tells you how the result is grouped, in words close to dplyr's. options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE) silences it (an explicit TRUE or FALSE always wins). With the option unset, dplyr's rule applies: the message appears only when summarise() is called from the global environment (top-level or interactive use), not from inside a function or package (a testthat test, or a verb such as tally.tbl_gpu() that calls summarise()).

.by

Optional grouping columns for this call only (tidyselect), run on the GPU. Groups come out in the order each .by combination first appears in .data, not sorted as after group_by() (see ".by group order" below). The result is always ungrouped. .groups can't be combined with .by, and supplying .by when .data is already grouped is an error, as in dplyr.

Value

A tbl_gpu object with one row per group containing the grouping columns and computed aggregations.

Details

Supported aggregation functions

  • sum(x) - Sum of values. Over an integer or logical x the result is an integer, as in dplyr; if it leaves R's integer range (+-(2^31 - 1)) dplyr returns a double, and so does tbl_gpu. Which one it is depends on the data, which a lazy plan (its schema is fixed before it runs) can't know, so a lazy summarise() of an integer sum(x) runs at the verb, like an eager one: the pending steps run first (a plan break, see cuplyr.plan_break) and the result is a lazy table with nothing pending. The same goes for a lazy min()/max() of an integer. A sum() of a logical x stays in the plan: it can only overflow with more than 2^31 TRUE rows in a group, and then raises a cuplyr_error_sum_overflow error at collect().

  • mean(x) - Arithmetic mean

  • min(x) - Minimum value

  • max(x) - Maximum value. min() and max() of a string column run on the GPU only when Sys.getlocale("LC_COLLATE") is "C" or "POSIX": the GPU compares bytes, while R uses the session's collation, so under any other collation they run in dplyr on the CPU.

  • n() - Count of rows in each group

  • sd(x) - Standard deviation

  • var(x) - Variance

  • median(x) - Median value, of a double, Date or POSIXct column. The median of an integer or logical column is of the column's type or a double depending on each group's count, and runs in dplyr on the CPU.

  • quantile(x, probs) - A single quantile, probs one number in [0, 1], with R's default type = 7. Other forms run in dplyr on the CPU.

  • n_distinct(x) - Count of distinct values, NA counted as its own distinct value by default

  • first(x) / last(x) / nth(x, n) - The first/last/nth value in the group's current row order

  • any(x) / all(x) - Logical reductions with R's three-valued logic

On the GPU, mean() and median() of a Date are floored to whole days with a cuplyr_warning_fractional_date warning, where dplyr keeps the fractional Date.

Some argument types run in dplyr on the CPU: a factor column under any aggregation but n_distinct(); an integer64 column under sum(), mean(), min(), max(), sd(), var(), median(), quantile(), any() and all() (its n_distinct(), first(), last() and nth() run on the GPU); and a Date or POSIXct column under any aggregation but min(), max(), mean(), median(), first(), last(), nth() and n_distinct().

Aggregation sub-expressions

column is not limited to a bare column name: any expression that filter.tbl_gpu() and mutate.tbl_gpu() run on the GPU is computed as a hidden temporary column first, then aggregated. This covers comparisons and logic (sum(carb > 3 & wt < 4), any(carb > 3)), arithmetic (mean(hp / wt)), and math functions (mean(sqrt(hp)), sum(carb %% 2 == 0)), nested to any depth: the same functions listed in mutate.tbl_gpu. A comparison or logical sub-expression is summed as TRUE/FALSE -> 1/0, as in R (sum(c(TRUE, TRUE)) is 2L), and stays logical inside any()/all(). Any other expression is evaluated by dplyr on the CPU.

column may also be (or contain) a window function call, e.g. last(cumsum(v)), sum(v - lag(v, default = 0)), mean(cumsum(v) - lag(cumsum(v))): the window function is computed per group first (over each group's own row order, with the same window functions mutate.tbl_gpu() runs on the GPU), and the aggregation then reduces that per-row result, as dplyr does. This applies to the argument of one aggregation; several aggregation calls in one expression are combined as described in the next section.

Arithmetic around reducers

An expression may combine reducer calls with arithmetic, comparisons, math functions and constants, and may read the result of an earlier expression: mean(x) + 1, sum(x) / n(), max(x) - min(x), mean(x) - qnorm(.975) * sd(x) / sqrt(n()), sum(cumsum(x)) - mean(y), s = sum(x), m = s / n(). Each reducer call is aggregated as above (a repeated call once), and the rest is computed on the one-row-per-group result with mutate.tbl_gpu()'s expressions, so the result has dplyr's types and NA values, with three exceptions. Math with no real value (sqrt(mean(x)) of a negative mean) is NaN without R's "NaNs produced" warning. A power can differ from R's in the last bit (var(x)^0.5 of 9 is 2.9999999999999996, where R computes 3 in extended precision), as in mutate.tbl_gpu(). An integer sum() that leaves the integer range in some group is a double in every group, so sum(x) + 1L gives a value in a group whose sum still is an integer where dplyr warns about the overflow and gives NA.

These stay with dplyr (the fallback notice names the reason, see cuplyr-fallback): a function of the group's rows around a reducer (lag(mean(x)), cumsum(sum(x))); ^ whose exponent is not a constant other than 0, NA and an infinity (R's NA^0 and 1^NA are 1, the GPU's are NA); ^ with an odd or non-integer exponent (mean(x)^3, max(x)^0.5, (-mean(x))^-1) unless its base is n(), n_distinct(), sd() or var() (R's power of a -Inf or -0, which max() of an empty group or -mean(x) of a zero mean gives, is not the GPU's: (-Inf)^0.5 is NaN in R, Inf on the GPU); &, | or ! of anything but a logical or an integer (R reads a double's NaN there as NA, and a string is R's error); if_else() or case_when() with a condition that is not a logical expression; a column of the input outside a reducer (mean(x) + x, dplyr's "must be size 1" error); a reducer that reads a name an earlier expression assigned (x = sum(x), t = sum(x)); an expression that reads the name of a later expression (mean(x) + k, k = sum(y): dplyr still sees the variable k there); count() inside an expression; a name assigned twice. A reducer inside a quosure spliced into the expression ({{ stat }}, !!quo) is computed in the quosure's own environment.

NA handling

mean()/sum()/min()/max()/sd()/var()/median() follow R's na.rm = FALSE default: if a group holds any NA in the aggregated column, that group's result is NA (summarise(m = mean(x)) is NA for a group with one NA in x), as in dplyr. Pass na.rm = TRUE (e.g. sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)) to leave the NA values out. n() counts every row, NA or not, as dplyr's n() does.

When na.rm = TRUE and a group's aggregated column is entirely NA, the result is base R's value for an empty vector, as in dplyr: sum() -> 0, mean() -> NaN, min() -> Inf, max() -> -Inf (with base R's warning "no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf" / "... max; returning -Inf", as dplyr shows it, for double and integer input alike; only when some group meets it), sd()/var()/median() -> NA.

Over an integer column, dplyr makes the whole min()/max() result column a double as soon as any group needs that empty-vector value, and keeps it integer otherwise; cuplyr does the same. Because that type depends on the data, a summarise() with an integer min()/max() runs immediately even on a lazy table (pending operations are computed first), and the result's schema reflects the real type. A 0-row input also counts as an empty group: ungrouped, summarise() returns one row of empty-vector reductions (n() 0, mean() NaN, sum() 0, min() Inf, ...); grouped, the result has no rows but an integer min()/max() is typed double, as in dplyr.

quantile() is different, as in base R's quantile(): with na.rm = FALSE (the default), an NA in the group is an error ("missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE"), not an NA result. Pass na.rm = TRUE to compute the quantile over the non-NA values.

n_distinct() counts NA as its own distinct value when na.rm = FALSE (the default, as dplyr's n_distinct() does): n_distinct(c(1, 2, NA, 2)) is 3. Pass na.rm = TRUE to leave NA out of the count.

first()/last()/nth() use dplyr's na_rm= spelling (underscore, not na.rm): na_rm = FALSE (the default) never skips an NA when picking the first/last/nth value (so the result can itself be NA); na_rm = TRUE skips NA values, returning the first/last/nth non-NA value in the group (or NA if the group has none).

any()/all() follow R's three-valued logic: any(x) is TRUE if any element is TRUE (whatever NAs there are), NA if there's no TRUE but at least one NA (with na.rm = FALSE, the default), else FALSE; all(x) is FALSE if any element is FALSE, NA if there's no FALSE but at least one NA (with na.rm = FALSE), else TRUE. na.rm = TRUE drops NA values first, as base R's any()/all() do (an all-NA group with na.rm = TRUE is FALSE for any() and TRUE for all()).

Ungrouped summarise

If .data is not grouped, summarise will compute aggregations over all rows, returning a single-row table.

No expressions

summarise(.data) with no expressions follows dplyr: ungrouped, it returns a one-row table with no columns; grouped, it returns the distinct group keys (one row per group, in group_by()'s ascending, NA-last order) and peels one grouping layer per .groups; with .by, it returns the distinct .by combinations in first-appearance order.

Tables with no columns

A GPU table can't hold rows without columns, so a zero-column tbl_gpu keeps its row count in R. What that covers: tbl_gpu(), dim(), collect()/as_tibble(), compute()/collapse(), group_by()/ungroup(), select()/relocate(), distinct(), zero-dot summarise() (1 x 0), summarise() with dots (in dplyr on the CPU, so n() counts correctly), slice() and its helpers, bind_rows()/bind_cols() of zero-column tables only, filter()/filter_out() (dplyr runs the call on a table of the same height, so row_number() and n() see its rows), mutate()/transmute() that leave no column (every column set to NULL), cross_join() and joins with by = character() where a side has no columns, the set operations of two zero-column tables, vctrs operations (vec_size(), vec_slice(), ...), reframe() with a zero-column data frame result, dplyr_row_slice(), and adding a column with $<-/[[<-. Binding a zero-column table that has rows to one with columns raises an error instead of returning a wrong row count.

Redefining columns

An expression named like a grouping column replaces that key in place (same position, the expression's type; the table stays grouped by that name). An expression that mentions a name an earlier expression created (or a name created twice) sees the new value, as in dplyr. When that expression is arithmetic around reducers and earlier results (m = s / n()) it runs on the GPU (see above); a reducer that reads the name (x = sum(x), t = sum(x)) or a repeated name runs in dplyr on the CPU.

Group order

group_by(g) |> summarise(...) returns groups in dplyr's group_by() order: ascending, NA last, strings in the C locale, FALSE < TRUE, factors in level order. count() and tally() give the same order.

.drop = FALSE

On a group_by(.drop = FALSE) grouping with a factor key, or on a table whose group keys are fixed (a .drop = FALSE table after filter(), semi_join(), slice(), ..., or a .preserve = TRUE slice), every group of group_data() gets a row, empty ones included, holding each expression evaluated on an empty vector (n() 0, sum() 0, mean() NaN, min() Inf with base R's warning, ...); with no expressions the result is the keys of every group. Such a call materializes a lazy table on the GPU (the row count is data-dependent). The result is regrouped with the input's .drop. Three shapes differ from dplyr or leave the GPU: min()/max() of a Date or POSIXct column is NA for an empty group (dplyr's Inf/-Inf cannot be held by a GPU timestamp column; an uploaded non-finite Date or POSIXct is NA as well, with the warning described in tbl_gpu()), mean() of a Date or POSIXct column is NA for an empty group where dplyr gives a NaN Date/POSIXct, and min()/max() of a character column runs the whole call on the CPU when a group is empty.

.by group order

summarise(.by = ) gives one row per distinct .by combination, in the order that combination first appears in .data, as dplyr does: summarise(tibble(g = c("b", "a", "b")), n = n(), .by = g) returns g in the order c("b", "a"), not c("a", "b"). group_by(g) |> summarise(...) sorts its groups instead. On the GPU this is one grouped summary, and its peak GPU memory is that of the group_by() form plus up to 12 bytes a row.

See also

group_by.tbl_gpu for grouping data, collect.tbl_gpu for retrieving results

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Simple aggregation over all rows
  total <- gpu_mtcars |>
    summarise(avg_mpg = mean(mpg)) |>
    collect()

  # Grouped aggregation
  by_cyl <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl) |>
    summarise(
      avg_mpg = mean(mpg),
      max_hp = max(hp),
      count = n()
    ) |>
    collect()

  # Multiple grouping columns
  by_cyl_gear <- gpu_mtcars |>
    group_by(cyl, gear) |>
    summarise(
      mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
      min_wt = min(wt)
    ) |>
    collect()
}
#> `summarise()` has regrouped the output by dropping the last grouping variable.
#> Summaries were computed grouped by cyl, gear.
#> Output is grouped by cyl.
#> Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message, or `.groups = "keep"`/`"drop"` to retain/drop every grouping level.
